name: Maria Pia Bridge
short: The 1877 railway arch bridge by Gustave Eiffel and Théophile Seyrig; it was replaced by the São João Bridge in 1991.
long: The Maria Pia Bridge was Gustave Eiffel's first major bridge and an outstanding monument of 19th-century engineering. Its crescent wrought-iron arch, with a 160-metre span, was the longest single-arch span in the world when it was built. The single-track bridge served the Lisbon–Porto line for more than a century, until the São João Bridge replaced it in 1991. It is no longer in service, but it remains part of the Douro valley skyline.
history:
In 1875 the Royal Portuguese Railway Company announced a competition for a bridge to carry the Lisbon–Porto line. The river here is fast, rises up to 20 metres in flood, and has a gravel bed, so piers in the water were impossible and a central span of about 160 metres was required.

Gustave Eiffel's design was the cheapest of the four proposals considered and was approved. Construction began on 5 January 1876; winter floods halted the work, which resumed in March 1877. The bridge was inaugurated on 4 November 1877 in the presence of King Luís I and Queen Maria Pia of Savoy, after whom it is named.

The structure uses a two-hinged crescent wrought-iron arch with a 160-metre span, then the longest single-arch span in the world, longer than the Eads Bridge arch at St Louis. The bridge is about 353 metres long and 60 metres above the water.

It was a single-track bridge, and over time load and speed restrictions turned it into a bottleneck. Rail service ended in 1991, when trains moved to the new São João Bridge; as early as 1990 the American Society of Civil Engineers recognised it as an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark. The bridge is closed today but remains part of the cityscape.
facts: Inaugurated on 4 November 1877; construction started on 5 January 1876.
Its 160 m central arch was the world's longest single-arch span at the time.
It was Gustave Eiffel's first major bridge, with calculations by Théophile Seyrig.
Single-track; replaced by the São João Bridge and decommissioned in 1991.
Recognised as an ASCE International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark in 1990.
tip: The best views are from the Ribeira quay and from the Dom Luís I Bridge, where the whole arch is visible. The bridge is closed to traffic, so admire it from a distance.
